claims.text: Adding a small amount of tungsten or molybdenum to phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloys will improve glass-forming ability.
Adding a small amount of tungsten or molybdenum will enhance the thermal stability of the amorphous state.
The proposed addition is 2–5 atomic percent tungsten or molybdenum.
The modified alloy is to be rapidly quenched to form an amorphous structure.
The transition-metal addition will enhance atomic packing efficiency.
The transition-metal addition will increase atomic-size mismatch.
Enhanced packing efficiency and atomic-size mismatch will increase the energy barrier for crystallization.
Tungsten or molybdenum atoms will disrupt the local atomic structure.
The local structural disruption will increase resistance to crystallization.
The addition will stabilize the amorphous phase thermodynamically.
The addition will stabilize the amorphous phase kinetically.
The modified alloy will have a lower critical cooling rate than the alloy without the addition.
The modified alloy will have a higher crystallization temperature than the alloy without the addition.
The modified alloy will have a larger supercooled-liquid region than the alloy without the addition.
Additions above about 10 atomic percent may cause phase separation or crystallization during quenching and eliminate the improvement.
The effect may be less pronounced in alloys that already have high glass-forming ability.
The concentration range that optimally improves glass-forming ability and amorphous-state stability is uncertain.
